On 26 March 1929 Charles E. Mitchell, head of National City Bank in New York, announced that his bank would put up $25 million to lend to stock buyers on margin, whatever the Federal Reserve wanted.

The Fed had warned member banks the month before to stop lending for speculation. A sharp stock fall on 25 March had pushed rates for these loans to 20 percent and scared the market. Mitchell's money calmed it, and prices climbed on, to the peak of September. He was also a director of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which is why his defiance was so striking.

Mitchell, nicknamed "Sunshine Charlie", had built National City into a big seller of stocks and bonds to ordinary customers, through its securities arm. Banks were then mixing deposits with investment dealing.

After the crash he was a symbol of Wall Street's excess. He resigned in 1933 and was questioned by the Pecora hearings, where he admitted the bank's loose lending and sales. His story fed into the Glass-Steagall Act, which separated commercial and investment banking.
